Abstract 25

Wastewater based epidemiology (WBE) uses concentrations of infectious agent targets in wastewater to 26

infer infection trends in the contributing community. To date, WBE has been used to gain insight into 27

infection trends of gastrointestinal diseases, but its application to respiratory diseases has been limited 28

to COVID-19. Here we report Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) genomic RNA can be detected in 29

wastewater settled solids at two publicly owned treatment works (POTWs). We further show that its 30

concentration in settled solids is strongly associated with clinical positivity rates for RSV at sentinel 31

laboratories across the state in 2021, a year with anomalous seasonal trends in RSV disease. Given that 32

RSV infections have similar clinical presentations to COVID-19, can be life threatening for some, and 33

immunoprophylaxis distribution for vulnerable people is based on outbreak identification, WBE 34

represents an important tool to augment current RSV surveillance and public health response efforts. 35

36

Keywords: RSV, Respiratory Syncytial Virus, wastewater-based epidemiology, sludge, settled solids, virus 37

38

Synopsis: Respiratory Syncytial Virus RNA concentrations in settled solids from wastewater treatment 39

plants are associated with state-wide RSV clinical positivity rates. 40

Introduction 44

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a single-stranded, - sense RNA, enveloped virus that infects the 45

respiratory tract of humans. RSV infections are usually self-limiting in healthy individuals but can 46

become severe, particularly for infants and immunocompromised or elderly individuals. Symptoms 47

include congestion, dry cough, fever, and trouble breathing in severe cases. Up to 1-2% of infants under 48

6 months with RSV are hospitalized, and RSV is responsible for up to a third of hospitalizations for acute 49

respiratory infections (ARI) in children <5 in the United States1. RSV is reportable to public health 50

officials in some locations in the United States, but many RSV infections are not identified because 51

people do not require or seek care and testing is not always done when patients encounter the 52

healthcare system. Given the similarities in presentation between COVID-19 and RSV, the challenge in 53

obtaining data on RSV in communities, and the high risk associated with infection in infants, there is a 54

need to better understand RSV incidence among US populations. 55

56

Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is a population health monitoring approach that uses 57

concentrations of pathogenic agents in wastewater to gain insight into infection rates in the contributing 58

community2. Using wastewater to understand community infection rates is a passive method that has 59

the benefit of capturing inputs from an entire community without a participation burden. WBE has been 60

used to gain insight into community infection rates of non-enveloped viruses including poliovirus3, 61

norovirus4, and hepatitis A5, which are excreted in stool of infected individuals and transmitted via the 62

fecal-oral route. Widespread implementation of WBE since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic 63

shows strong associations between SARS-CoV-2 RNA in wastewater influent6–8 and settled solids 9–11 and 64

laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 incidence rates. Although COVID-19 is primarily a respiratory disease, 65

SARS-CoV-2 RNA is excreted in stool of those infected12–14. To date WBE has not been used to provide 66

information on infection rates of other respiratory viral diseases such as RSV. 67

68

Population monitoring for RSV can help establish guidelines for diagnostic testing and preventative 69

measures. RSV is a seasonal outbreak disease with infections typically peaking in October and 70

transmission ongoing through May, however seasonality can differ across regions of the United States 71

and from year to year15. The 2020/2021 RSV season in the United States was substantially delayed 72

during the COVID-19 pandemic and in June 2021 the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 73

issued a health advisory warning of unexpected interseasonal RSV outbreaks16. Limited RSV 74

immunoprophylaxis products are currently available to those at high risk and administered on a monthly 75

basis depending on both personal risk and outbreak status17. Identifying outbreaks is thus important for 76

targeting administration of these monoclonal antibodies, and for ongoing vaccine trials for multiple 77

promising candidates and eventually targeting vaccine administration. 78

79

To investigate whether RSV is present in stool of infected patients and thus potentially present in 80

wastewater, we conducted a literature review (see Supporting Information (SI)). We identified two peer- 81

reviewed papers that tested for the presence of RSV genomic RNA in stool samples. von Linstow et al.18 82

studied 44 children admitted to a hospital over a 6 month period with an ARI caused by RSV or human 83

metapneumovirus. They collected one stool sample at enrollment and then weekly for three weeks from 84

each child. RSV viral RNA was detected using quantitative RT-PCR in 5 of 165 total stool samples. The 85

five positive stool samples were obtained from five unique children with RSV infections. Shedding in 86

stool only occurred within the first week of illness. In 2017, a case report by Akbari et al.19 detected RSV 87

RNA in stool. Three stool samples were collected from a 12-month old female presenting with acute 88

gastroenteritis and tested for respiratory viruses and gastrointestinal bacteria using a complete 89

92

The goal of this study is to investigate whether RSV can be detected in wastewater and, if so, whether its 93

concentration is associated with clinical RSV positivity rates. Previous work indicates that enveloped 94

viruses partition to the solids in wastewater where their concentrations are enriched orders of 95

magnitude over the liquid phase20,21. We therefore focused our analysis on wastewater solids at two 96

publicly owned treatment works (POTWs) in a highly urbanized region of the San Francisco Bay Area, 97

California, USA. We first designed and tested a custom digital droplet (dd-)RT-PCR assay that targets the 98

N gene of RSV A and RSV B. We then applied the assay to settled solids collected biweekly to three days 99

per week at the POTWs between January and mid-November 2021. The resultant concentrations are 100

compared to the limited information publicly available on RSV infections in the State of California. 101

102

Methods 103

Assay development for RSV. A digital RT-PCR assay was designed to target the N gene of RSV. RSV A and 104

RSV B genomes were downloaded from NCBI. The assay was developed in silico using Primer3Plus 105

(https://primer3plus.com/). The parameters used in assay development (that controlled sequence 106

length, GC content, and melt temperatures) are provided in Table S1. 107

108

Primers and probe sequences were screened for specificity in silico using NCBI Blast, and then tested in 109

vitro against a virus panel (NATtrol™ Respiratory Verification Panel NATRVP2-BIO, Zeptomatrix, Buffalo, 110

NY) that includes several chemically inactivated intact influenza viruses, parainfluenza viruses, 111

adenovirus, rhinovirus, metapneumovirus and several coronaviruses, and “wild-type” gRNA from SARS- 112

CoV-2 strain 2019-nCoV/USA-WA1/2020 (ATCC® VR-1986D™). A mixture of RSV B (NATtrol™ RSV 113

positive Control NATRSV-6C, Zeptometrix) and RSV A (from NATtrol™ Flu Verification Panel NATFVP- 114

NNS, Zeptometrix) was also included as a positive control. RNA was extracted using Chemagic™ Viral 115

DNA/RNA 300 Kit H96 for Chemagic 360 (Perkin Elmer, Waltham, MA). RNA was used undiluted as 116

template in digital droplet PCR singleton assays. The concentration of targets used in the in vitro 117

specificity testing was between 103 and 104 copies per well; each target from the respiratory panel was 118

run in a single well, and the SARS-CoV-2 gRNA was tested in 8 wells. 119

120

Wastewater samples. Two publicly owned treatment works (POTWs) that serve populations of Santa 121

Clara County, California, USA (San José-Santa Clara Regional Wastewater Facility, RWF) and San Mateo 122

County, California, USA (Silicon Valley Clean Water, SVCW) were included in the study. RWF and SVCW 123

serve approximately 1,500,000 and 220,000 people, respectively; further descriptions of these POTWs 124

can be found in Wolfe et al.22 . 125

126

Samples of approximately 50 mL of settled solids were collected by POTW staff using sterile technique in 127

clean, labeled bottles. Grab samples were taken at SVCW. At RWF, POTW staff manually collected a 24 h 128

composite sample21. Samples were immediately stored at 4°C, transported to the lab, and processed 129

within 6 hours of collection. 130

131

Samples were collected daily for a larger COVID-19 wastewater surveillance effort starting in November 132

202022 , and a subset of these samples are used in the present study and were chosen to span the period 133

prior to and including increasing RSV incidence in the state23. Although RSV incidence usually peaks in 134

the winter, the 2020-2021 was an anomalous year with limited to no RSV cases and increasing cases 135

beginning in the summer (Figure 1). One sample was analyzed every other week during January, 136

February, and March; one sample was analyzed per week in April and May, and then three samples per 137

included in the analysis for a total of 180 samples. 139

140

RNA was extracted from the 10 replicate aliquots of dewatered settled solids as described in Wolfe et al. 141

22,24,25. RNA was subsequently processed immediately (within 24h of sample collection) to measure 142

concentrations of the N gene of SARS-CoV-2, pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV), and bovine 143

coronavirus (BCoV) recovery using digital droplet RT-PCR methods reported by Wolfe et al. 22,26.  PMMoV 144

is highly abundant in human stool and wastewater globally27,28  and is used here as an internal recovery 145

and fecal strength control for the wastewater samples29 . BCoV was spiked into the samples and used as 146

an additional recovery control; all samples were required to have greater than 10% BCoV recovery. 147

During the initial measurement, RNA extraction and PCR negative and positive controls were included to 148

ensure no contamination as described in Wolfe et al.22. Extracted RNA samples were then stored at - 149

80°C between 4 and 300 days before they were analyzed for the RSV N gene and SARS-CoV-2 N gene in a 150

multiplex digital RT-PCR assay; each of the 10 replicate RNA extracted were run in its own well, and the 151

10 wells were merged for analysis. The SARS-CoV-2 N gene was run a second time in all samples to test 152

for RNA degradation during storage (no to minimal degradation was observed, see SI). Wastewater data 153

and MIQE reporting details30 are available publicly at the Stanford Digital Repository 154

(https://purl.stanford.edu/ck044th0182); results below are reported as suggested in the EMMI 155

guidelines31. 156

157

ddRT-PCR 158

For the assay specificity testing, the RSV assay was challenged against target (RSV A and B) and non- 159

target (other respiratory viruses) viral gRNA. Each PCR plate contained positive controls and negative 160

PCR no template controls (NTC). PCR positive controls for each target assayed on the plate were run in 8 161

wells, and NTC were run in 8 wells. Positive controls for the assays consisted of a mixture of RSV A and B 162

gRNA. 163

164

The ddRT-PCR methods applied to wastewater solids to measure the SARS-CoV-2 N gene, PMMoV, and 165

BCoV are provided in detail elsewhere, including details relating to EMMI31 guidelines and are not 166

repeated here22. Here, we provide methods for the multiplexed SARS-CoV-2 N and RSV N gene assays 167

which have not been reported previously. For this multiplexed assay, ddRT-PCR was performed on 20 µl 168

samples from a 22 µl reaction volume, prepared using 5.5 µl template, mixed with 5.5 µl of One-Step RT- 169

ddPCR Advanced Kit for Probes (Bio-Rad 1863021), 2.2 µl Reverse Transcriptase, 1.1 µl DTT and primers 170

and probes at a final concentration of 900 nM and 250 nM respectively. Primer and probes for the RSV A 171

& B N gene were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT, San Diego, CA) (Forward primer: 172

CTCCAGAATAYAGGCATGAYTCTCC, Reverse Primer: GCYCTYCTAATYACWGCTGTAAGAC, Probe: 173

TAACCAAATTAGCAGCAGGAGATAGATCAG (5’ HEX/ZEN/3’ IBFQ)). 174

175

Droplets were generated using the AutoDG Automated Droplet Generator (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA). PCR 176

was performed using Mastercycler Pro (Eppendforf, Enfield, CT) with with the following cycling 177

conditions: reverse transcription at 50°C for 60 minutes, enzyme activation at 95°C for 5 minutes, 40 178

cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 30 seconds and annealing and extension at 61°C for 30 seconds, 179

enzyme deactivation at 98°C for 10 minutes then an indefinite hold at 4°C. The ramp rate for 180

temperature changes were set to 2°C/second and the final hold at 4°C was performed for a minimum of 181

30 minutes to allow the droplets to stabilize. Droplets were analyzed using the QX200 Droplet Reader 182

(Bio-Rad). A well had to have over 10,000 droplets for inclusion in the analysis. All liquid transfers were 183

performed using the Agilent Bravo (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). 184

a sample to be recorded as positive, it had to have at least 3 positive droplets. Each wastewater sample 187

was run in 10 replicate wells, and each 96-well PCR plate of wastewater samples included PCR positive 188

controls for each target assayed on the plate in 1 well, PCR NTCs  in two wells, extraction negative 189

controls (where no sample was added to the extraction kit) in two wells, and one extraction positive 190

control (containing SARS-CoV-2 gRNA) in one well. PCR positive controls consisted of gRNA of SARS-CoV- 191

2 (strain 2019-nCoV/USA-WA1/2020, ATCC® VR-1986D™) and RSV B and A gRNA (NATRSV-6C and RSV A 192

from NATtrol™ Flu Verification Panel, Zeptometrix). 193

194

Results from replicate wells were merged for analysis. Thresholding was done using QuantaSoft™ 195

Analysis Pro Software (Bio-Rad, version 1.0.596). In order for a sample to be recorded as positive, it had 196

to have at least 3 positive droplets. For the wastewater samples, three positive droplets corresponds to 197

a concentration between ~500-1000 cp/g; the range in values is a result of the range in the equivalent 198

mass of dry solids added to the wells. 199

200

For the wastewater samples, concentrations of RNA targets were converted to concentrations per dry 201

weight of solids in units of copies/g dry weight using dimensional analysis. The dry weight of the 202

dewatered solids was determined by drying25. The total error is reported as standard deviations and 203

includes the errors associated with the Poisson distribution and the variability among the 10 replicates. 204

206

Clinical data in RSV. The weekly fraction of samples positive for RSV (hereafter “RSV positivity rate”) 207

from sentinel laboratories in the State of California are publicly available from the California Department 208

of Public Health website 209

(https://www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/CID/DCDC/Pages/Immunization/Influenza.aspx)23. Sentinel 210

laboratories are hospital, academic, and private laboratories, and public health laboratories in the 211

Respiratory Laboratory Network situated throughout California. 212

213

Statistical analysis. RSV N gene concentrations were compared between POTWs using Kendall’s tau and 214

Wilcoxon Sign Tests as data were not normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk normality test, p<0.05). Weekly 215

average RSV N gene concentrations and weekly average RSV N gene concentrations normalized by 216

PMMoV were calculated for each week of 2021 through 12 Nov 2021 to match the frequency of RSV 217

positivity rate reporting; the weekly average was calculated using all available data (between 1 and 3 218

data points). We tested the null hypothesis that weekly average wastewater concentrations were not 219

associated with weekly positivity rates from sentinel laboratories using Kendall’s tau. We used linear 220

regression to determine the rate of change of RSV positivity with RSV wastewater concentrations. 221

Measurements below the detection limit were replaced with 500 copies/g (the approximate detection 222

limit). All statistical analyses were implemented in R studio (version 1.4.1106). 223

224

Results and Discussion 225

RSV Assay specificity.  In silico analysis indicated no cross reactivity between the RSV assay and 226

deposited sequences in NCBI. When challenged against the respiratory virus panel and SARS-CoV-2 227

gRNA no cross reactivity was observed; and the assay amplified gRNA from both RSV A and RSV B. 228

Positive controls and NTCs run on the sample plate were positive and negative. These results suggest 229

that the RSV ddRT-PCR assay is specific to both RSV subtypes. 230

231

RSV RNA concentrations in wastewater solids. All positive and negative controls were positive and 232

negative respectively, indicating assays performed well and without contamination. BCoV recoveries 233

an efficient and acceptable recovery of RNA during RNA extraction (Figure S1). 235

236

Concentrations of the RSV N gene in wastewater solids ranged from non-detect to 6.2x104 copies/g dry 237

weight. At both POTWs RSV levels were non-detect until late June at which time concentrations began 238

to increase through the last sample collected in mid-November (Figure 1). Concentrations of RSV RNA 239

were positively and significantly correlated at the two POTW (Kendall’s tau = 0.52, p<10-12). Paired, log10- 240

transformed concentrations were not different between POTWs (paired, Wilcoxon signed rank test V = 241

988, p=0.9385, N = 90). Given the close proximity of the POTWs (located 40 km from each other), the 242

similar concentrations may suggest similar RSV infection rates in their sewersheds. 243

244

The temporal trend in RSV RNA concentrations in settled solids mirrors state-wide trends in RSV 245

positivity rate, identifying an infection pattern that differs from usual seasonal trends. Weekly averaged 246

RSV RNA concentrations at each POTW were strongly correlated with the weekly positivity rate (tau = 247

0.77, p<10-10 for RWF, tau = 0.65, p<10-7 for SVCW, N=39). We repeated the analysis normalizing RSV 248

RNA concentrations by PMMoV and found similar results. Normalizing by PMMoV can serve to correct 249

for sample-to-sample changes in RNA extraction efficiency, concentrations during storage, or differences 250

in the fecal strength of the wastewater 22,32 (Figure S2). A 1 log10 increase in RSV RNA is associated with 251

an 0.08 (RWF) and 0.05 (SVCW) increase in RSV positivity rate (r2 = 0.89, p <10-15 for RWF; r2 = 0.70, p 252

<10-10 for SVCW, N = 39) (Figure 2). The results are unchanged if the RSV concentrations are normalized 253

by PMMoV. 254

255

Concentrations of RSV RNA in wastewater solids reported are similar to concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 256

RNA in wastewater solids when laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 incidence rates are between 1/100,000 257

and 10/100,00022. The positivity rates used herein were calculated using data from sentinel laboratories 258

through the state rather than from the sewershed areas, and thus do not provide direct information on 259

population incidence rates. Additional work to compile RSV incidence data in the sewersheds may allow 260

for estimates of disease burden associated with RSV in wastewater beyond outbreak identification and 261

trends. Understanding how RSV RNA in wastewater relates to incidence rates will also require a better 262

understanding of RSV shedding from infected individuals. In particular, there is no quantitative data on 263

RSV RNA concentrations in stool of infected patients and the potential for sputum or other bodily 264

secretions to contribute RSV RNA to wastewater should be considered. 265

266

The consistent detection of RSV in wastewater beginning during a known outbreak and strong 267

associations between RSV RNA concentrations at the POTWs and state-wide trends in positivity rates at 268

sentinel laboratories supports the idea that RSV RNA concentrations can be used to identify outbreaks 269

and infer infection trends within contributing populations. Wastewater surveillance may be especially 270

useful for diseases like RSV where clinical surveillance is challenging, yet tracking of outbreaks is 271

required to initiate public health response. Wastewater concentrations may allow insight into when 272

infection rates begin to rise, and may be especially useful for identifying unusual season trends in 273

diseases like that observed for RSV in 2021. This work suggests that regular monitoring for RSV in 274

wastewater can be useful to identify and target response to outbreaks. Success in monitoring for both 275

COVID-19 and RSV suggests that additional efforts should be made towards wastewater monitoring for 276

existing and novel enveloped respiratory viruses. 277
